author: amanda-berry-smith
fields.title: Amanda Smith: An Autobiography (For Teens)
fields.description: Amanda Berry Smith was born owned — a slave in Maryland — and became a preacher who crossed oceans alone. This teen retelling of her own memoir doesn’t flinch: slavery, grief, and prejudice are here, and so is a fierce, honest faith. Straight talk for anyone who’s ever been told they don’t rank, that God is for other people, or that the problems are too big to touch.

qa.question: Was Amanda Smith really born into slavery?
qa.answer: Yes. She was born owned in Maryland in 1837, and her father, Samuel Berry, worked for years — days for the woman who owned him and nights making brooms and mats — to buy first himself and then his wife and children out of slavery.

qa.question: How much schooling did she get?
qa.answer: Almost none — about three months in total. She taught herself to read by cutting large letters out of newspapers and arranging them into words on the windowsill.

qa.question: How did a Black woman with no money become a preacher who traveled the world?
qa.answer: She had no ordination, no salary, and no church board behind her, and most ministers of her day opposed women preaching. She went anyway, convinced God had called her, and ended up ministering across the United States, Britain, India, and eight years in West Africa.

qa.question: Does this teen edition cover the hard parts of her life?
qa.answer: Yes, honestly. It deals directly with slavery, racism, poverty, and the deaths of her husbands and children — the difficult material a younger children’s version leaves out — without dwelling on gruesome detail.

qa.question: What did she mean by “belonging to royal stock”?
qa.answer: Amanda came to believe she was a child of God and carried herself with dignity no matter how others ranked her. In one English church she looked proud strangers in the face so they could see, as she put it, that she was “of the royal black.”

qa.question: Who was little Bob?
qa.answer: Bob was a young boy in West Africa whose own father asked Amanda to raise him and teach him about God. Though she was sick and had no money, she took him into her home as her own child after sensing God tell her, “You do what you can, and where you leave off, God will raise up somebody to do the rest.”

qa.question: Did Amanda found an orphanage in this book?
qa.answer: Not in this story. The orphanage she later became known for came after this memoir; in these pages her care for children is personal — taking individual children like Bob and her Bassa girl Frances into her own home.

qa.question: What is the biggest thing a teenager can take from her life?
qa.answer: That a bad deal doesn’t have to be a dead end. Amanda faced injustice she couldn’t undo and grief she couldn’t reverse, and she kept trusting God and doing the next brave thing in front of her.

fields.title: Born Owned, Bought Free
fields.body_html:
“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” — John 8:36 (ESV)

Amanda Berry was born in Maryland in 1837, and she was born owned. In the country of her birth a Black child could be bought and sold like a horse or a sack of grain, handed over as part of a bride’s dowry, worked for a whole lifetime and never paid a cent. That was the law, and law is a cold word for something that broke families apart on purpose. Amanda was too young to remember the worst of it. But she never forgot that her freedom had a price, and that someone paid it.

Her father, Samuel Berry, paid it. He belonged to a woman who let him earn money on the side, so he did the math on his own life and got to work. He finished his day’s labor for her, then made brooms and husk mats by candlelight to sell at market. In harvest season he worked her fields all day, walked three or four miles after dark to work other fields until one or two in the morning, slept an hour, and did it again. First he bought himself. Then he started buying his wife and children — thirteen children in all — because a man could only save so fast.

Money alone was not going to be enough, though. The family Amanda’s mother belonged to did not want to sell. What changed things was a death and a stubborn old woman’s prayers. Amanda’s grandmother had prayed for years that her grandchildren would be free, and she meant it — she used to slip into the bushes to, as they said, “tell Jesus” about it. Meanwhile a young mistress named Celie was converted at a camp meeting, to her family’s disgust, and then fell sick with typhoid fever. Dying, she gathered her family and asked one thing: that they let Samuel buy Amanda’s mother and the children. Three days running she asked it, until they promised. Amanda later said she had “been bought twice, and set free twice,” and figured that gave her a good right to shout.

Here is what you should not miss in that story. The evil in it was legal. Respectable, church-going people owned human beings and slept fine. One of the men in the area who hunted down runaways for the reward money was a class leader in his church. So do not assume that because something is normal, or lawful, or done by decent-seeming people, it is therefore right. Whole societies can agree on a lie and build courts and customs to protect it.

Amanda’s father did not wait for the country to come to its senses. He worked in the dark for years to buy back what should never have been for sale, and her grandmother prayed as if God actually intended to answer. You will meet injustice that is bigger than you — rules you cannot repeal, wrongs you cannot undo by yourself. That is exactly the situation the Berrys were in, and they did two things anyway: they told the truth about it, and they kept working and praying toward freedom instead of shrugging and calling it fate. Freedom that costs someone that much is worth taking seriously in your own life, too.

One thing to do: find out the real cost of something you have always just had. Ask a parent or grandparent what they, or people before them, gave up so your life could be what it is — the move, the job, the sacrifice, the prayers. Write down one thing you learn. You cannot honor a gift you never bothered to understand.

fields.title: The Man in the Bed
fields.body_html:
“Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.” — Proverbs 24:11 (ESV)

After the Berrys were free they settled on a farm in Pennsylvania, and their house became one of the main stations on the Underground Railroad — the secret network that moved people escaping slavery north toward Canada. This was not safe, quiet charity. There were men in the nearby town who made their living catching runaways for the reward, and they watched Amanda’s family closely. Her father would work all day, sleep two hours, then walk fifteen or twenty miles in the dark to carry someone — sometimes a man, sometimes a mother and child — to the next safe place, and get home just before dawn to start work again.

One night the catchers tricked their way in. A well-dressed stranger knocked, claiming to be hungry and headed to the camp meeting, and Amanda’s father fed him. It was a setup. Soon men were pounding at the door demanding the runaway they said he was hiding, and when they rushed in they beat her father and trampled over the children asleep on the floor. Amanda’s mother ran to defend him and a man slashed at her with a knife; it caught the iron door of the stove instead of her body. Amanda thanked God for that stove door for the rest of her life. The man they were after leapt from an upstairs window and ran, but a bloodhound caught him. They took him back into slavery, and the family never heard of him again.

Another morning her father was outside feeding the pigs when he saw four men on horseback coming — too late to warn his wife properly. He just called out, “Mother, I see four men coming; do the best you can.” Inside, a man was hiding upstairs. In seconds she brought him down and hid him flat in the bed under the straw mattress, laid her own small son on top, and made up the room. When the sheriff and his men searched, she calmly threw open the door, pulled back the covers to show the little boy, and even said, “Look under the bed as well.” They laughed and left. The man was safe, and they got him off to Canada.

Notice that Amanda’s parents did not do this because it was easy or because anyone would praise them. They did it in the dark, at real risk of prison, violence, and death, for strangers whose names they often never learned. Their faith was not only a feeling they had on Sundays; it was a set of dangerous decisions they made on ordinary weeknights. When the Bible says to rescue those being dragged toward death, they took it as an instruction with an address on it — their own front door.

You probably will not be asked to hide a fugitive. But you will notice people being mistreated, excluded, cornered — and you will feel the pull to look away, because getting involved is awkward and costly and none of your business. The Berrys teach you that “the best you can” is a real answer. You do not have to fix everything. You have to do the brave, specific thing in front of you, now, before the moment passes.

One thing to do: the next time you see someone getting singled out or shut out — a new kid, a target of a group chat, someone being pushed around — do one concrete thing to stand with them within the hour. Sit by them, speak up, walk them out. Not later, when it is safe. Then.

fields.title: Learning to Read in the Cold
fields.body_html:
“The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple.” — Psalm 119:130 (ESV)

Add up all the schooling Amanda Smith ever got and it comes to about three months. Three months, across her whole childhood. It was not because she was slow or lazy. It was because school, for a Black girl in her time and place, was something handed out in leftovers.

Her first real lessons she gave herself. Her father brought home newspapers, and Amanda cut out the large letters, laid them on the windowsill, and asked her mother to help her arrange them into words. She never forgot the day she first read a line on her own — “The house, the tree, the dog, the cow.” She called the other children over to show them. She thought she knew everything.

Later she and her brother had to walk about five miles to a school that took a few Black children. One bitter winter morning the snow was deep and the cold was dangerous. Her mother was afraid she would freeze and did not want her to go; Amanda insisted, bundled up, wearing her brother’s heavy boots. Halfway there the cold got into her and, wrapped so tightly she could barely move, she nearly froze on the road. She was too stubborn, and too afraid of being kept home, to turn back. By the time she reached the schoolhouse door she could not open it and could not speak; a boy had to let her in, and people worked over her a long time before she came to.

And after a walk like that? At the school the white children got their full lessons first. If any time was left over, the Black children got a turn. Many days Amanda made that miles-long trip and got exactly one lesson — squeezed in while everyone else was packing up their lunch pails to go home.

Sit with how unfair that is, because it is important not to smooth it over. She was just as capable and just as hungry to learn as any child in that room, and she was made to wait for the scraps of the school day because of her skin. That is the injustice she grew up inside of. And here is the part worth admiring: it did not kill her hunger to learn. She taught herself letters off a windowsill. She read her Bible until it argued back at her. As a grown woman she crossed oceans, spoke to crowds, and kept a diary on three continents — this person the system had decided did not deserve a full day of school.

You may have gotten a bad deal in some direction — a school that is failing, teachers who wrote you off, a home where studying is hard, a subject people said your “kind” of person does not do. That deal is real, and naming it is not making excuses. But Amanda draws a hard line between a bad deal and a dead end. What was handed to her was a bad deal. What she did with it was refuse to let it become a dead end. Nobody could give her a fair classroom. Nobody could stop her from cutting letters out of a newspaper.

One thing to do: pick one thing you have decided you “can’t” learn because school made it miserable — reading real books, math, writing, an instrument. Teach yourself the very first piece of it this week, on your own, for fifteen minutes, the way Amanda taught herself letters. Prove to yourself the door is not actually locked.

fields.title: The Argument That Almost Won
fields.body_html:
“See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.” — Colossians 2:8 (ESV)

As a teenager Amanda thought of herself as a believer, but a casual one — she said her prayers, kept out of trouble, and figured she would get serious about God someday. Then she picked up a book. It was written as a debate between a Christian minister and an unbeliever, and she opened it completely confident: “I know the Christian minister will win.”

He did not. Or at least, the book was rigged so it looked like he did not. The way it was written, the skeptic’s questions were sharp and clever and given the most space, and the minister’s answers gradually shrank and lost ground. By the last page, Amanda said, the unbeliever “seemed to gain all the ground.” And here is the thing she was honest about: she could not remember the Christian’s arguments at all anymore. But the skeptic’s case was “stamped on my memory and spirit.” She had read one book and quietly stopped being sure God even existed.

What makes this story so useful is what happened next. She did not become a bold, happy atheist. She became afraid and secretly miserable. She was scared someone would find out. She kept reading more of the same material “to strengthen me in my new light,” and every book pulled the knot tighter. She wanted out and could not find the door. She was, in her own word, snared.

She got free almost by accident. Her aunt came to visit — a plain, no-nonsense believer like Amanda’s mother — and as they walked across a long bridge the aunt said something about how wonderfully God had made the sky and the water. Amanda saw her chance to unload and fired her best skeptical shot: “How do you know there is a God?” Her aunt did not argue. She turned, looked at Amanda with a look that “went through me like an arrow,” stamped her foot, and said she would not even talk to a girl raised the way Amanda had been who would say such a thing. And that broke the snare. Amanda felt it lift in that instant. She was always convinced that if her aunt had argued point by point, she would have stayed trapped for good.

Take two things from this. First, what you read and watch and scroll is not neutral, and it is not harmless just because it is “only ideas.” A single well-made argument — or a hundred short ones fed to you by an app that knows what keeps you watching — can move you somewhere you never chose to go, and you may not even notice you have moved. Amanda was intelligent and sincere and got captured anyway. Being smart is not the same as being safe.

Second, the way out of a snare of ideas usually is not out-arguing it alone at one in the morning. It is often a real person who knows you and loves you and will not debate you — who simply refuses to accept the frame you have fallen into. That kind of person is worth having, and worth being.

One thing to do: look honestly at the one voice, channel, or feed that has quietly shaped how you see the world lately. Ask yourself: is it making me more truthful, or just more sure of things I never examined? Then take it to one older person you actually trust and say what you have been thinking out loud. Snares grow in secret.

fields.title: Down in the Cellar
fields.body_html:
“You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart.” — Jeremiah 29:13 (ESV)

Amanda had wanted to be a Christian for as long as she could remember. The problem was that she wanted to do it her own way — quietly, respectably, on her own terms. She had planned exactly how her conversion would go. She would not make a scene, would not go forward at any altar, would not be one of “those people” who wept and shouted. She was proud of her strong will. When Amanda said she would not do a thing, people said you might as well try to move a mountain.

So she prayed and struggled for months and got nowhere, because every time God got close she ran into her own will. She kept comparing herself to people she considered worse than she was. She was, she admitted later, so proud and so unsure how to actually trust God that she once found herself praying to the sun and the moon and the stars to carry her message to Jesus, because she felt too sinful to speak to him directly.

It came to a head on an ordinary afternoon while she was ironing. A thought pressed in on her — she recognized later it was the tempter — running through her whole record: You have prayed. You have been sincere. You have fasted and read your Bible and really wanted this. And God still has not saved you. You might as well give up. And Amanda, exhausted, agreed: “Well, I guess I will just give it up.” Then another voice, quieter, said, “Pray once more.” And something in her rose up and put the weight on one word: “I WILL.” She said she felt it from the top of her head all the way through her.

She set the kettle on, laid the table nearly ready so nobody would call her, and went down into the cellar on her knees — genuinely believing, in her desperation, that she had made a vow and God might strike her dead. “I have come down here to die,” she prayed, “and I must have salvation this afternoon or death.” She prayed the same broken prayer over and over. And then she came to the end of herself, of every plan and every clever wording, and simply said, “O, Lord, if Thou wilt help me I will believe Thee” — and in the act of saying she would, she did. The burden rolled off. Light and joy poured through her. She ran up out of the cellar new.

Here is what is striking for anyone who has ever tried to fix their own life by sheer willpower: her strong will was not what saved her. It was, for years, the exact thing in the way. She was determined to come to God without giving up control, without being embarrassed, without doing it any way but hers — and that determination kept her stuck. The breakthrough came the moment she stopped negotiating and actually trusted him.

You will spend real energy protecting your image and your control. There are things you will not do because of how they would look, apologies you will not make, help you will not ask for, because your pride has drawn a line. Amanda’s cellar is where she found out that the line was the prison. Seeking God “with all your heart” meant, for her, dropping the conditions.

One thing to do: name the one condition you have quietly attached to getting serious about God — “as long as I don’t have to look weird, apologize, give that up, or admit I was wrong.” Say it plainly to yourself. Then, on that exact point, drop the condition and act as if you trust God more than your own image.

And Amanda, exhausted, agreed: “Well, I guess I will just give it up.” Then another voice, quieter, said, “Pray once more.” And something in her rose up and put the weight on one word: “I WILL.” She said she felt it from the top of her head all the way through her. She set the kettle on, laid the table nearly ready so nobody would call her, and went down into the cellar on her knees — genuinely believing, in her desperation, that she had made a vow and God might strike her dead. “I have come down here to die,” she prayed, “and I must have salvation this afternoon or death.” She prayed the same broken prayer over and over. And then she came to the end of herself, of every plan and every clever wording, and simply said, “O, Lord, if Thou wilt help me I will believe Thee” — and in the act of saying she would, she did. The burden rolled off. Light and joy poured through her. She ran up out of the cellar new. Here is what is striking for anyone who has ever tried to fix their own life by sheer willpower: her strong will was not what saved her. It was, for years, the exact thing in the way. She was determined to come to God without giving up control, without being embarrassed, without doing it any way but hers — and that determination kept her stuck. The breakthrough came the moment she stopped negotiating and actually trusted him. You will spend real energy protecting your image and your control. There are things you will not do because of how they would look, apologies you will not make, help you will not ask for, because your pride has drawn a line. Amanda’s cellar is where she found out that the line was the prison. Seeking God “with all your heart” meant, for her, dropping the conditions. One thing to do: name the one condition you have quietly attached to getting serious about God — “as long as I don’t have to look weird, apologize, give that up, or admit I was wrong.” Say it plainly to yourself. Then, on that exact point, drop the condition and act as if you trust God more than your own image.

fields.title: Buying Back Frances
fields.body_html:
“Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute.” — Psalm 82:3 (ESV)

Amanda’s younger sister Frances was born free, in Pennsylvania, to free parents. That should have been the end of the danger. It was not. When Frances was small she went to live with an aunt in Maryland, and things went badly — the aunt was harsh, Frances ran away to a family that treated her better, and in the chaos of the Civil War years, when Black people were being seized and sold if they could not instantly prove they were free, a freeborn child was simply sold anyway. For forty dollars. To a man for a term of ten years.

Amanda was working as a servant for six dollars a month when the word reached her. She borrowed fifty dollars against her wages and went — traveling into a slave state as a Black woman during a war to get her sister back. She reached the area and started walking the miles to the farm, alone, having eaten nothing all day. She was afraid to stop at houses for even a drink of water. At one fine house with a pump right there in the yard she asked an old woman on the porch for water and was told, “No, no; go on, go on.” Amanda nearly fainted, then prayed that God would just take the thirst away — and, she said, it left her completely, and she walked on another mile in the sun.

When she reached the farm and found Frances, the man who “owned” her sister raved and swore and refused to let a freeborn girl go for less than the forty dollars he had paid. It was outrageous — Amanda had no legal duty to pay a cent for a person who was never lawfully anyone’s property. But there was no one to swear for Frances in court, no protection coming, and a furious man with a horsewhip in his hand. So Amanda paid. She handed over the money, and Frances left with the single dress she stood in and one more under her arm. Amanda spent years working off that debt.

Be honest about how this story makes you feel, because the feeling is the point. It is infuriating. Amanda did everything right and still had to buy back her own free sister from a man with no right to sell her, because the law and the people around them would not protect a Black girl. Sometimes doing the loving thing means paying a price that is completely unjust — a price you should never have been handed. Amanda paid it because Frances mattered more to her than the principle of the thing.

That is a hard, grown-up kind of love, and you will need to understand it. There will be times when the fair solution is simply not available — when standing up for someone, or cleaning up a mess that was not yours, or protecting a person who is cornered, costs you money, time, comfort, or credit you did not owe. The immature response is, “That’s not fair, so I won’t.” Amanda’s response was to count the person as worth more than the unfairness. She never pretended it was fair. She just decided Frances came first.

One thing to do: think of one person in your life who is being treated unfairly and cannot fix it alone — a sibling, a friend, someone at school. Do one thing to help them this week that costs you something and that you technically “don’t have to” do. Love that only shows up when it is fair and convenient is not the kind Amanda’s family practiced.

fields.title: When the Grief Came
fields.body_html:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (ESV)

It would be dishonest to tell Amanda Smith’s story as one victory after another. Her life held a staggering amount of loss. Her first husband went off to the Civil War and never came back. She buried children — a baby taken by sickness one hard summer while she worked as a cook far from home, and later a little boy, Tom Henry, after weeks of suffering. Out of thirteen brothers and sisters, only she and two others lived to adulthood. Her second marriage, which she had hoped would finally give her a Christian home, turned out lonely and painful; her husband had misled her about his plans and had little patience with her faith.

And through much of it she was poor and working herself to the bone. She took in washing to survive, and she describes standing at the washtub straight through the night — starting at six one morning and working to six the next — so tired she would lean her head on the window ledge to sleep a few minutes, then keep going by lamplight until dawn. This is the real texture of her life: grief and exhaustion stacked on top of each other, with no obvious relief coming.

For a long time her instinct was to try to escape the trials — to pray her way around them, to reach a place in life where the pain would finally stop. Then an older woman named Mother Jones came by one morning while Amanda was crying over the washtub, heartbroken about her husband’s coldness. Amanda poured out all the good things she had done and how unfair it all was. Mother Jones did not tell her the pain would end. She said something else: that what Amanda needed was “enduring grace.” Not a life with no trouble — the strength to stand up inside the trouble. Amanda realized she had spent all her energy “planning to get out of trials, instead of asking God for grace to endure.”

That is a genuinely different idea about faith, and it is worth slowing down for. A lot of people, when they are hurting, are really asking God to make the hard thing disappear — heal it, reverse it, get me out. And sometimes he does. But Amanda learned that the deeper, more reliable gift is grace strong enough to carry you through the thing that does not disappear. The verse she leaned on did not promise her power instead of weakness. It promised power made perfect in weakness — right in the middle of it, not after it is gone.

You are going to lose things and people, some of them badly, some of them unfairly, some of them soon. That is not pessimism; it is just true, and nobody your age is served by pretending otherwise. When it comes, you will be tempted to measure God by whether he removes the pain fast enough, and to feel abandoned when he does not. Amanda would tell you to ask a better question: not only “God, take this away,” but “God, hold me up in this.” She buried more than most of us ever will and did not stop trusting — not because it stopped hurting, but because grace turned out to be sufficient, exactly as promised.

One thing to do: think of a hard thing in your life right now that probably is not going to just vanish. Instead of only praying for it to be removed, start praying — out loud, honestly — for the strength to walk through it well. Then name one person who is grieving something and go sit with them, the way Mother Jones sat with Amanda.

fields.title: The Only One Standing
fields.body_html:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” — Galatians 3:28 (ESV)

One Sunday morning, after years of hunger for a deeper experience of God, Amanda felt strongly that she should go to Green Street Church in New York to hear a preacher named John Inskip. The whole walk there, doubts and fears crowded her — worries about her baby at home, fear of what her husband would say, one excuse after another to turn aside to a closer church. She kept walking.

She arrived worn out and sat a few seats from the door. And she was, as far as she could see, the only Black person in the building. That mattered to her, and she was honest about why. She wrote that she had always carried a kind of fear of white people — not that they would hurt her, exactly, but a deep unease, a sense that they were “there” and important and she was “here” and not. She had learned, growing up in service, to hold herself carefully, to know her place, to never make a scene where white people might see.

So as the sermon opened her up and God met her in a way she had been seeking for twelve years, a war started inside her. Wave after wave of joy rose in her and she wanted to shout for gladness — and every single time, a voice said: if you make a noise here, in front of all these white people, they will put you out. She sat on her hands. She held it in. Twice she felt the joy come and twice she smothered it out of fear. It nearly cost her the whole thing; she sank for a few minutes into real despair.

Then, standing there trembling, she heard words come to her, clear, from the corner of the church: there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. She said she had never really understood that verse before, but God made it plain to her in that moment. And when the closing hymn reached the line about the blood that cleanses from all sin, she stood up on shaking legs and shouted “Glory to Jesus” — out loud, in that room, the only Black woman in it. The preacher answered, “Amen, Glory to God.” Walking home afterward she said the white people she had always been afraid of “looked so small. The great mountain had become a molehill.”

Read that carefully, because it is not a small thing. A society had spent Amanda’s whole life teaching her that she was less — that she should shrink, stay quiet, stay in the back, never draw attention in a white room. And what finally broke that fear was not a slogan about self-esteem. It was one line of Scripture landing with power: in Christ, the categories the world ranks you by — your race, your class, your gender — do not decide your worth. She was not a lesser person who should keep silent. She was one, fully and equally, with everyone in that room, before God.

You have absorbed messages about where you rank, too — from your school, your feed, the room you feel you have to shrink in. Some of you have been made to feel small for exactly the things Amanda was: your color, your money, your family, your body. Amanda’s morning at Green Street says the mountain that makes you feel small is often smaller than it looks, and that the truest thing about you is not your rank in anyone’s eyes but your standing before God, who counts you as one, not less.

One thing to do: name the room or situation where you make yourself small — where you go quiet, hide, and shrink because you feel like you do not rank. Next time you are in it, do one honest, ordinary thing you would normally suppress: speak up, take the seat, ask the question. Stand up, the way Amanda finally did.

fields.title: Go, and I Will Go with You
fields.body_html:
“Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.” — Exodus 4:12 (ESV)

When Amanda became convinced God was calling her to leave New York and go out preaching, everything about it was against her. She was a Black woman in a time when most ministers — including Black ministers — did not believe women should preach in public at all. She had no ordination. No church board stood behind her. No salary. No education to speak of. And she was being sent, of all places, to a town called Salem, New Jersey, where she did not know a single soul. When the sense came that she should go, she pushed back hard, asking God again and again to make it unmistakable, half hoping he would change his mind.

He did not, so she started getting ready with almost nothing. She needed to pay her rent and she needed shoes — her only pair was broken through the sole, and she knew wet feet in winter would make her sick. She did not tell anyone; she made her needs known only to God. She prayed for the money for shoes and, remarkably, told God she would trust him for them so completely that she “put them on as really as ever I put on a pair of shoes,” claiming them by faith before they existed. Days later an old man at a meeting pressed some money into her hand as she left. She got home, counted it — five dollars, the first time anyone had ever just handed her that much — and remembered: the shoes.

Then the doubts turned personal and mean. As she stood ironing, the accusation came: Jesus sent his disciples out two by two, and here you are going alone — people will say you are just going out to find a husband. That one stung, because she knew people would talk. She set down her iron, got on her knees, and asked God to send someone to go with her if she was meant to have a companion — and the answer that came was simply the promise he had already given: “Did I not tell you that I would go with you?” She had forgotten it. She got up in peace and went alone.

What should grab you here is how much Amanda had to lose and how little cover she had. She was not stepping out with a scholarship, a title, a team, and a safety net. She was a poor washerwoman defying what nearly everyone around her thought was proper, walking into a strange town on the strength of a conviction she could not prove to anyone. Every practical fact said stay home. She weighed the mockery, the loneliness, and the risk — and decided that obeying a God she could not see was safer than disobeying to keep herself comfortable.

You will face smaller versions of this constantly: the thing you are fairly sure is right to do, but that no one is requiring, no one is applauding, and plenty of people would find weird or presumptuous. “Who do you think you are?” is a powerful sentence, and it stops a lot of people cold. Notice that the accusation Amanda faced was not even about whether God had called her — it was about what people would say. She learned to tell the difference between God’s guidance and the crowd’s opinion, and to act on the first even when the second was against her.

One thing to do: identify one right thing you have been putting off mainly because of how it would look or what people might say — not because it is wrong, just because it is exposed. Take the first concrete step on it this week, alone if you have to. Do the thing you are fairly sure God would have you do, before the fear of looking foolish talks you out of it.

fields.title: Amanda Smith, the Washerwoman, Go to England?
fields.body_html:
“And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.” — Philippians 4:19 (ESV)

Years into her work, an English woman suggested Amanda come to England for a trip and some rest. Amanda’s first reaction was to laugh at the idea. “Go to England! Amanda Smith, the colored washwoman, go to England!” She decided she would not even pray about it. She figured she had to ask God for so many things she genuinely needed that she was not going to bother him about something as far-fetched as an ocean voyage. “It does well enough for swell people to go,” she thought, “not for me.”

But the sense that God actually wanted her to go kept growing, and so did her fear. Because underneath the “who am I?” was something more specific: Amanda was terrified of the sea. Her whole picture of the ocean was that it was always rough and deadly. She thought about the three thousand miles, about her daughter back home, about all the things that could go wrong, and she wrote a letter turning the trip down. She felt relieved the moment she dropped it in the mailbox — for a little while.

Then, that evening, a wave of darkness came over her that she could not shake. She locked her doors, turned the lamp low, got on her knees, and refused to sleep until she understood what was wrong. She went through everything she had said and done that day looking for some sin — nothing. Finally, quiet, she heard it plainly: “You are going about telling people to trust the Lord in the dark, to trust him when they cannot see him. You tell other people to do what you are not willing to do yourself.” And then the specific truth: “You are afraid to trust the Lord and go to England. You are afraid of the ocean.” Amanda said it took her breath away, because it was exactly, humiliatingly true.

That is worth stopping on, because it is a trap almost everyone falls into and almost no one notices. Amanda made her living, in a sense, telling people to trust God through things they could not see or control. And she had quietly exempted herself from her own message at the one point where it scared her. She was a hypocrite in the original sense — not a villain, just a person whose actions had not caught up to her words. What is admirable is that when God named it, she did not defend herself. She said, “Lord, that is the truth,” repented, and later crossed that ocean alone.

There is a second thing here for anyone who has ever felt too ordinary for anything. On the way, and once she arrived, proud and wealthy passengers looked down on the Black washerwoman traveling first class with no important reason and no one to meet her. Amanda did not argue with them or shrink. In one church she quietly turned and looked two well-dressed women “squarely in the face so they could see I was of the royal black.” She had come to believe she belonged to royal stock — a child of God — and she carried herself like it, whatever anyone thought.

So two questions for you. First: where are you telling other people — a younger sibling, a friend, a teammate — to be brave, honest, or faithful in a way you are privately dodging yourself? And second: where are you letting other people’s ranking of you convince you that big, good things are “for swell people, not for me”?

One thing to do: find the one place your words and your nerve do not match — the advice you give that you will not take. Do the scary thing you keep telling others to do, this week. Stop asking people to trust God in the dark from a spot where you have kept the lights on for yourself.
fields.body_text: “And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.” — Philippians 4:19 (ESV) Years into her work, an English woman suggested Amanda come to England for a trip and some rest. Amanda’s first reaction was to laugh at the idea. “Go to England! Amanda Smith, the colored washwoman, go to England!” She decided she would not even pray about it. She figured she had to ask God for so many things she genuinely needed that she was not going to bother him about something as far-fetched as an ocean voyage. “It does well enough for swell people to go,” she thought, “not for me.” But the sense that God actually wanted her to go kept growing, and so did her fear. Because underneath the “who am I?” was something more specific: Amanda was terrified of the sea. Her whole picture of the ocean was that it was always rough and deadly. She thought about the three thousand miles, about her daughter back home, about all the things that could go wrong, and she wrote a letter turning the trip down. She felt relieved the moment she dropped it in the mailbox — for a little while. Then, that evening, a wave of darkness came over her that she could not shake. She locked her doors, turned the lamp low, got on her knees, and refused to sleep until she understood what was wrong. She went through everything she had said and done that day looking for some sin — nothing. Finally, quiet, she heard it plainly: “You are going about telling people to trust the Lord in the dark, to trust him when they cannot see him. You tell other people to do what you are not willing to do yourself.” And then the specific truth: “You are afraid to trust the Lord and go to England. You are afraid of the ocean.” Amanda said it took her breath away, because it was exactly, humiliatingly true. That is worth stopping on, because it is a trap almost everyone falls into and almost no one notices. Amanda made her living, in a sense, telling people to trust God through things they could not see or control. And she had quietly exempted herself from her own message at the one point where it scared her. She was a hypocrite in the original sense — not a villain, just a person whose actions had not caught up to her words. What is admirable is that when God named it, she did not defend herself. She said, “Lord, that is the truth,” repented, and later crossed that ocean alone. There is a second thing here for anyone who has ever felt too ordinary for anything. On the way, and once she arrived, proud and wealthy passengers looked down on the Black washerwoman traveling first class with no important reason and no one to meet her. Amanda did not argue with them or shrink. In one church she quietly turned and looked two well-dressed women “squarely in the face so they could see I was of the royal black.” She had come to believe she belonged to royal stock — a child of God — and she carried herself like it, whatever anyone thought. So two questions for you. First: where are you telling other people — a younger sibling, a friend, a teammate — to be brave, honest, or faithful in a way you are privately dodging yourself? And second: where are you letting other people’s ranking of you convince you that big, good things are “for swell people, not for me”? One thing to do: find the one place your words and your nerve do not match — the advice you give that you will not take. Do the scary thing you keep telling others to do, this week. Stop asking people to trust God in the dark from a spot where you have kept the lights on for yourself.

fields.title: Let Your Men Keep Silence
fields.body_html:
“And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” — Acts 2:17 (ESV)

Amanda’s travels took her all the way to India, where she preached in packed churches and saw people come to faith. But not everyone welcomed her. In one city a group of Christians was deeply offended that a woman was preaching. They quoted Paul — “Let your women keep silence in the churches” — at her constantly. They wrote articles against her in the newspapers. They sent her letters loaded with Bible verses telling her to stop, even pointing out passages they wanted her to preach on instead.

Amanda had a rule about this kind of thing: “I never argue with anybody — just say my say and go on.” But one night she decided to take the subject head-on. The church was packed. She stood up, read out her text, and quoted — accurately, chapter and verse — a line from the very same passage her critics loved: “Let your men keep silence in the church.” She was making a sharp point. That instruction in First Corinthians was Paul telling a chaotic congregation that if there was no one to interpret what was being said, the speaker — man or woman — should be quiet so the meeting would not dissolve into confusion. It was about order, not about permanently silencing half the church. After that meeting, she noted, the newspaper articles stopped and the letters stopped, and she went on with her work.

Now, you can find Christians today who still disagree about exactly what women should and should not do in church, and that is a real conversation. But notice Amanda’s actual example, which is bigger than that one debate. Faced with people using Scripture as a weapon against her, she did not get loud, did not get bitter, and did not quit. She went back to the text itself, in context, calmly, and let it answer for her. She out-studied her critics instead of out-shouting them.

Earlier on that same long journey, in Paris, Amanda had watched a potter shape clay on a wheel. She saw how the potter had total control — he could turn one lump into a cup, then a pitcher, then a bowl, whatever he willed, and the clay never argued back. And she noticed the beautiful colors only came out after the pieces went through the furnace. Watching it, she prayed to be like that clay in God’s hands — even when the furnace came, to submit and “not dictate.” Those two pictures belong together. The furnace was the opposition, the prejudice, the constant fight to be allowed to do what God had called her to do. She did not demand a life without the furnace. She trusted the potter who was using it to make something.

Here is what to carry away. People will sometimes come at you with rules, verses, or “facts” bent into weapons — to shut you up, keep you down, or knock you off something you are supposed to be doing. The childish responses are to melt down or to fire back with more heat. Amanda models a third way: know your material better than they know theirs, stay calm, and keep going. And underneath that calm was the potter’s-clay trust — she was not fighting to control her own reputation; she had handed that to God and was free to just do the work.

One thing to do: the next time someone uses a “rule” or a twisted fact to shut you down on something you are sure is right, do not argue back louder — go learn the thing cold. Read the actual source, get the context, know it better than they do. Then say your say, calmly, and go on.

fields.title: Little Bob
fields.body_html:
“Princes shall come out of Egypt. Ethiopia shall hurry to stretch out her hands to God.” — Psalm 68:31 (WEB)

Amanda spent eight years in West Africa — far longer than the “trip” she had once been too afraid to take. She arrived weak with fever, buried friends, and worked without much money in a hard place. Early on she learned a lesson that shaped the rest of her time there. She wanted to start a work for local boys and began praying for money, running through a mental list of all the friends back in America who might send some. Weeks passed. No money came. Finally she asked God why, and the answer landed: “You are not trusting in Me, you are trusting in America; you are looking to America for help more than to Me.” She saw it instantly, let go of her American safety net, and told God she would trust him alone — and the help, from unexpected places, began to come.

That set up the story she called simply “How I Came to Take Little Bob.” Amanda had long wanted to raise and educate a boy, but the families she asked would not give up their children, and she had finally given up on the idea. Then in Cape Palmas two little boys used to hang around the gate, and she would share her leftover food with them and talk to them. She grew fond of one especially — Bob. One day, passing by, she stopped to put her hand on his head, and a man standing nearby called out to her. It was Bob’s father, Jack. In broken English he said something Amanda never forgot: “I be fool; I no sabe God. I don’t want my pick’n to be fool all same like myself.” He was asking her to take his son and teach him about God, because he did not want the boy to grow up knowing nothing, the way he felt he had.

Amanda’s honest reaction was reluctance. She was sick and weak, she had no money to support a child, and she knew a small boy would be a lot of work and responsibility. She kept telling Jack no, or not yet, and finally took it to God: “Thou knowest I have no money to support this child... But if Thou dost want me to take him, and wilt make it clear, it will be all right.” The answer came in two lines. First: “Is not Ethiopia stretching out her hands to God?” — a whole continent reaching out. Then, when she protested that she was so weak and did not know what she could do: “You do what you can, and where you leave off, God will raise up somebody to do the rest.” So she took Bob. His parents signed an agreement giving him to her to raise and educate as her own child.

Sit with that last promise, because it is the antidote to a very modern kind of paralysis. Amanda looked at an enormous need — a continent’s worth of children, poverty everywhere, her own weak body — and the size of it was a reason to do nothing. What freed her was not a plan to fix all of it. It was permission to do what she could and trust God with the rest. She did not have to be enough. She had to take the one boy in front of her.

You will feel this too. The problems are gigantic and you are one person with limited time, money, and energy, and it is tempting to conclude that since you cannot fix it, you might as well not start. Amanda’s whole life answers that. A father who bought his children out one at a time. A grandmother who prayed. A washerwoman who took one boy into her own home. None of them could do everything. All of them did what they could — and where they left off, God raised up somebody else to do the rest, including, eventually, a woman who almost stayed home because she was afraid of the sea.

One thing to do: pick one problem too big for you that you actually care about — someone lonely, something broken in your school or town, a need you keep scrolling past. Stop waiting until you can fix all of it. Do the one small thing you actually can do, this week, and trust God to raise up others where you leave off.
